newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Albright takes blunt message to Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Albright takes blunt message to Bosnia.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright flew to the Bosnian capital Sarajevo on Sunday to push for full compliance with the Dayton peace treaty, after reprimanding the presidents of Serbia and Croatia for failing to honour the agreement.

Albright met the Moslem, Croat and Serb members of the country's collective presidency as part of a U.S. effort to shore up the 1995 peace agreement, which ended four years of war in former Yugoslavia.
She was carrying a stern warning to Bosnian political leaders that the United States and European powers would impose penalites on any faction which violated provisions of the treaty.
Her visit coincides with growing international concern that the Dayton agreement could be unravelling, a year before the NATO-led peace force is due to withdraw.
Nationalist authorities in Bosnia, trying to seal the results of wartime "ethnic cleansing", have prevented refugees from returning to their homes and ignored other elements of the treaty.

Albright rebuked Bosnia's powerful neighbours on Saturday, demanding that Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic ensure the extradition of indicted war criminals and the safe return of refugees.
She called for Milosevic, a key signatory of the U.S.- brokered Dayton accords, to stop "stonewalling" and cooperate with the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

She specifically cited former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic, who still wields power in Serb-controlled territory, and three Yugoslav generals accused of atrocities near Vukovar during the 1991 Serb-Croat war.
Milosevic claimed he did not have enough information about the three generals but Albright said she gave him tribunal documents so "he has no excuses".
Albright had a tough meeting with Tudjman earlier in Zagreb and a direct face-off at a joint news conference.

As Tudjman looked on grim-faced, she said: "I believe it is the appropriate role of leadership of every country to provide moral direction ... and I asked President Tudjman to provide that kind of leadership."

She said she told Tudjman, who is up for reelection in two weeks' time, that he must prevent violence against Serb war refugees trying to return to Croatia and also cooperate with the war crimes tribunal at the Hague.
Albright was scheduled to fly by helicopter later on Sunday to the disputed northern town of Brcko, considered one the country's most volatile flashpoints.

Bosnian Serb authorities retain control of the town which they seized during the 1992-95 war. The Serbs are under pressure to allow Moslem and Croat refugees to return to their homes in Brcko, which lies along a strategic land corridor linking Serb-controlled territory to the west and east.

Albright planned to speak with American soldiers serving in the Stabilisation Force (SFOR) before heading to the northwestern town of Banja Luka, where she was due to hold talks with Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic.
